transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

I’m here because I just feel completely drained, like my body’s been emptied out. It’s not just “tired,” you know? Even doing small things feels like too much. Like walking from my car into the clinic today felt like it took everything I had, and at work even opening the EHR can feel like this huge task, like my arms and brain and everything are just heavy. I know that probably sounds dramatic, but it’s honestly been hard to get through basic stuff.
Have you been feeling down or depressed lately?

Yeah… I have. It kind of came after my energy just dropped off. At first I kept thinking maybe I was just tired or burnt out, but then it turned into this empty feeling most days, like there’s this hopelessness sitting there and I can’t really shake it.

And I keep thinking I’ve already messed everything up, especially with work and trying to get started in healthcare. Like I’m only 18 and I should be building toward something, but instead it feels like I’ve already ruined my future before it even really started. It’s hard not to feel down when that’s the thought running in my head all the time.
After even small amounts of physical or mental activity, do your symptoms get noticeably worse afterward?

Yeah, it does. Like, even really small things just wipe me out. Walking from my car into the clinic today sounds like nothing, but by the time I got inside I felt like I’d spent all my energy already. And at work, even just opening the EHR or trying to focus on one basic task can feel like this huge thing, like my body and my brain are both running on nothing. It’s not normal tiredness where I can just push through it — it feels like I’m completely drained after barely doing anything.
When you wake up after a full night of sleep, do you still feel unrefreshed?

Yeah… definitely. Even when I technically sleep a long time, I don’t wake up feeling rested. Lately it’s been all over the place, honestly. There was a stretch where I’d only sleep like two or three hours and somehow still feel wired, like my body wouldn’t shut off. But now it’s more like I either wake up way too early, before it’s even really morning, and I’m already sick with worry, or I sleep half the day and still feel completely exhausted.

It’s frustrating because I’ll think, okay, if I just sleep more maybe I’ll feel better, but then I wake up and it’s like nothing got restored. My body still feels heavy, my head still feels foggy, and it’s almost like the sleep didn’t count.
During that time when you were sleeping only two or three hours, did you still feel unusually energetic despite so little sleep?

Yeah… during that stretch, that’s exactly what was weird about it. I’d only sleep like two or three hours, and I should’ve been completely dead the next day, but instead I still felt wired, like my body was running on something that wasn’t normal sleep. It didn’t feel restful or calm, just like I couldn’t shut down.

And now it’s kind of flipped. Lately I either wake up before dawn already feeling sick with worry, or I end up sleeping half the day and still feel exhausted, like none of it actually helped.
During that stretch when you were sleeping only two or three hours, did you feel unusually confident or on top of the world?

Yeah… I did. At the time it didn’t feel like “confidence” in a normal way, though. It felt like I could see everything more clearly than everyone else, especially at work.

I really believed I understood patient care better than the nurses and even the managers. Like, I’d be watching how things were done and thinking, why is nobody listening to me, I can fix this, I can make this whole place run better. I remember feeling like if they just let me explain it, or if someone actually took me seriously, I could change the whole system — not just one small thing, but the whole way people were being cared for.

Looking back, that sounds kind of… too much. But in the moment I was completely sure of it. I felt like I was the one who really got it.
During that period when you felt wired and unusually confident, were you taking on a lot more projects or doing much more than usual?

Yeah… I was doing way more than usual. Like, not just being “busy,” but I was suddenly trying to fix everything at work all at once.

I started making these workflow plans, like writing out how things should be done differently, how people should communicate better, how patient care could be faster or safer or more organized. And I’d get really intense about it, like I’d think of something at night and then message coworkers after hours because I felt like it couldn’t wait until the next shift. At the time I thought I was being helpful, but looking back I can see it was probably a lot for people.

I was also offering to train people, which is embarrassing to say because I wasn’t even that far ahead of them. Like I’d barely learned something myself and then I’d act like I could teach everyone the “better” way to do it. I really believed I had this bigger understanding of how everything should work.

And I kept taking on extra tasks too. I’d volunteer for stuff, jump into things, try to help with everything, and then it got messy because I couldn’t even finish my basic responsibilities properly. There were times where I was stretched so thin that I didn’t feel like I was doing the normal tasks safely or carefully enough, which scares me now when I think about it. At the time, though, I just felt like I had to keep going and do more.
During that wired, overly confident period, did it get serious enough that you were hospitalized or it caused major problems at work, school, or with other people?

Yeah… it definitely got serious. I wasn’t hospitalized, like admitted overnight, but work basically stopped me from continuing. It wasn’t just that people thought I was annoying or overdoing it — it got to the point where I couldn’t keep up with the actual patient-support tasks I was supposed to be doing.

I’d start documentation and then either get pulled into some bigger idea in my head about how it all needed to be fixed, or I’d lose track of what I was documenting, and that scared people. It scares me now too, because documentation has to be accurate and safe, and I wasn’t staying focused enough. I couldn’t finish things the way I needed to, or I’d jump from one task to another like everything was urgent.

Employee health ended up pulling me from work and sending me for an emergency evaluation. That was… really embarrassing. I remember feeling angry at first, like they just weren’t understanding me, but looking back, I can see why they did it. I wasn’t functioning normally there.

And outside of work, I had been trying to prepare seriously for my CNA certification, but I had to stop. I just couldn’t keep up with studying or organizing myself enough to actually prepare in a real way. I’d have all these plans, but I couldn’t follow through. So yeah, it caused major problems.
